explanations.answer: Each official is watched by one higher up
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the Teacher gives. He says "one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them." (Ecclesiastes 5:8) So there's a whole ladder of watchers, and every rung has somebody looking down at it. I think that's his way of saying: don't fall over in shock when you see this, friend.

explanations.answer: The poor will soon rise up against them
explanations.explanation: The Teacher never says the poor will rise up. He says one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them (Ecclesiastes 5:8). That's his reason for not being astonished. Nobody in this verse is starting a revolution, they're all just being watched from above.

explanations.answer: The king will judge them all in time
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the verse doesn't mention the king judging anybody. It says one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them (Ecclesiastes 5:8). That chain of officials is the whole reason he gives. A king does show up in the very next verse, but he's out in the fields, not on a judge's seat.

Yep, the Teacher says "The produce of the earth is taken by all…" (Ecclesiastes 5:9). Everybody gets a piece of it. Kind of like a fresh tray on my counter, friend: I turn around for one second and the whole tray has a crumb problem.

explanations.answer: It is kept by the farmers
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say the farmers get to keep it. It says the produce of the earth is taken by all (Ecclesiastes 5:9). Everybody is reaching in, not just the folks who worked the ground. I think the farmers might have wanted a word about that.

explanations.answer: It is kept by the officials
explanations.explanation: The officials were in the verse before, but this verse isn't about them hoarding the harvest. The Teacher says the produce of the earth is taken by all (Ecclesiastes 5:9). That's everybody, from top to bottom. Nobody gets to hold the whole thing.
True! The Teacher says "the king himself profits from the fields." (Ecclesiastes 5:9) Even the guy at the very top is getting something out of that dirt. Nobody is above the harvest, friend.

Actually, it's true. The Teacher says "the king himself profits from the fields." (Ecclesiastes 5:9) So the king is right there with everybody else, getting something out of the harvest. The man wears a crown and still needs the dirt.

That's the word. "He who loves money is never satisfied by money…" (Ecclesiastes 5:10) Loving money is like a bottomless cookie jar, friend, and I would know. You reach in, it's empty, and somehow you still want to reach in again.

Close in feeling, but that's not the word. The Teacher says the one who loves money is never satisfied by it (Ecclesiastes 5:10). He's not saying the money wrecks the man here. He's saying the man keeps wanting more and never gets to enough.

The Teacher doesn't say the money changes anybody here. He says "He who loves money is never satisfied by money…" (Ecclesiastes 5:10). The problem isn't a new man, it's the same man still hungry. Every time he gets more, there's still room for more.

Right on. "When good things increase, so do those who consume them…" (Ecclesiastes 5:11) The more that comes in, the more mouths show up to help with it. I've watched a cookie box do this with my own eyes.

Envy makes sense, but the Teacher doesn't say it. He says "When good things increase, so do those who consume them…" (Ecclesiastes 5:11). So the ones multiplying are the ones using it up. Nobody's glaring from the corner, they're all eating.

You'd think more stuff means more guards, but that's not what the verse says. The Teacher says "When good things increase, so do those who consume them…" (Ecclesiastes 5:11). The crowd that grows is the crowd doing the consuming. Guarding doesn't come up at all.

That's it, and it's a funny little punchline. The Teacher asks "what then is the profit to the owner, except to behold them with his eyes?" (Ecclesiastes 5:11) All that stuff, and the owner's big reward is looking at it. That's like baking twelve dozen and getting to stand there and stare.

That's what you'd expect, but the Teacher says the opposite. Since those who consume the good things increase, the profit to the owner is only "to behold them with his eyes" (Ecclesiastes 5:11). So no extra pile for himself. Just a nice view.

Rest sounds nice, but the verse never gives the owner that. The Teacher asks what the profit is "except to behold them with his eyes?" (Ecclesiastes 5:11). Looking is all he gets. The rest part comes up in the very next verse, and it goes to somebody else.
Sleep is the word. "The sleep of the worker is sweet…" (Ecclesiastes 5:12) The rich man's abundance, though, "permits him no sleep." Honestly, friend, a good pillow beats a big pile of anything.

Nice thought, but bread isn't in this verse. The Teacher says the worker's sleep is sweet, while the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep (Ecclesiastes 5:12). The comparison is about rest, not what's on the table. One man is snoring and the other one is wide awake.

Pay isn't what the Teacher talks about here. He says "The sleep of the worker is sweet…" and the rich man's abundance permits him no sleep (Ecclesiastes 5:12). The one with the sweet part is the worker, and what's sweet is his sleep. His paycheck doesn't get a mention.
Not quite, friend. The Teacher says the worker's sleep is sweet "whether he eats little or much" (Ecclesiastes 5:12). So a big meal isn't the key. The sweet sleep doesn't depend on a full table.

Right, it's false. The Teacher says "The sleep of the worker is sweet, whether he eats little or much…" (Ecclesiastes 5:12). Little or much, the sleep is sweet either way. It's the rich man's abundance that keeps him awake.

explanations.answer: There is nothing to pass on
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The wealth is lost in a failed venture, "so when that man has a son there is nothing to pass on." (Ecclesiastes 5:14) The son is there, but the inheritance isn't. I think that's a heavy picture, so let's let it sit for a second.

explanations.answer: The son has to repay the debt
explanations.explanation: A debt isn't in the verse. The Teacher says the wealth is lost in a failed venture, so when the man has a son there is nothing to pass on (Ecclesiastes 5:14). The problem is an empty hand, not a bill. Nothing gets handed down at all.

explanations.answer: The son has to work the fields
explanations.explanation: The fields came up earlier, but they aren't part of this verse. The Teacher says that when the man has a son, "there is nothing to pass on." (Ecclesiastes 5:14) That's all the text says about the son. It doesn't tell us what he ends up doing.

Not this time, friend. The Teacher says "He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands." (Ecclesiastes 5:15) Not a little, not a handful, nothing. Even my biggest batch can't ride along in my mustache.

Correct, it's false. The Teacher says a man came from his mother's womb, and will depart "naked as he arrived. He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands." (Ecclesiastes 5:15) Hands empty going out, same as coming in. Nothing makes the trip.

Gains is the word. The Teacher asks, "What does he gain as he toils for the wind?" (Ecclesiastes 5:16) It's a question with a pretty clear answer sitting in it. You can't hold wind, friend, and I have tried to stamp it.

Fear is a good guess, but it's not the word here. The Teacher asks, "What does he gain as he toils for the wind?" (Ecclesiastes 5:16) The question is about what the man gets out of all that work. Fear isn't what he's weighing.

Owing sounds money-ish, but that's not the word. The Teacher asks, "What does he gain as he toils for the wind?" (Ecclesiastes 5:16) He's asking about what the man gets from all that work. Debts aren't in the verse.

That's the one. The Teacher says "all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger." (Ecclesiastes 5:17) It's a gloomy table, friend. I think it's the kind of meal where even the dessert looks sad.

That sounds lovely, but it's the opposite of the verse. The Teacher says "all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger." (Ecclesiastes 5:17) No crowd of friends is mentioned at all. It's a dark and heavy way to eat.

Peace and honor would be nice, but that's not what the Teacher says. He says "all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger." (Ecclesiastes 5:17) That's the man toiling for the wind. His meals are anything but peaceful.

explanations.answer: To eat and drink and enjoy his work
explanations.explanation: Yes! The Teacher says it's good and fitting "to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him…" (Ecclesiastes 5:18) Enjoy the work you're given, friend. Even the stamping part, even the cleanup.

explanations.answer: To store up wealth for his son
explanations.explanation: That's not what the Teacher calls good and fitting. He says it's "to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun…" (Ecclesiastes 5:18) Earlier he told us what happens to wealth when there's nothing to pass on (Ecclesiastes 5:14). Here the good is enjoying the work and the day.

explanations.answer: To keep working until he has enough
explanations.explanation: The Teacher already said the lover of money is never satisfied (Ecclesiastes 5:10), so "enough" never shows up on that road. What he calls good and fitting is "to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun…" (Ecclesiastes 5:18) The satisfaction comes inside the work, not after some finish line.
True. The Teacher speaks of "the few days of life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18). Few days is a good reason to enjoy them. Nobody needs to spend those days staring at the ceiling.
It's actually true. The Teacher says "the few days of life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18). Few is his word for them. That's part of why he says to find satisfaction in the labor now.

Enjoy fits the first blank. The Teacher says God "has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor." (Ecclesiastes 5:19) God does the enabling here. The man doesn't have to squeeze the joy out of it on his own.

Gift fits the second blank. The Teacher ends the verse with "This is a gift from God." (Ecclesiastes 5:19) And that's good news for anybody holding a mixing spoon, friend. Enjoying your work is something God gives.

Hoard doesn't fit. The Teacher already called "wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner" a grievous evil (Ecclesiastes 5:13). In this verse, God enables a man to enjoy his riches and wealth. Hoarding is the problem, enjoying is the gift.

Burden is the opposite of what the verse says. The Teacher says "This is a gift from God." (Ecclesiastes 5:19) The word is gift, and it sits right at the end of the verse. Joy in your labor isn't a weight to carry.

Counting is what the money lover does, but it's not what the verse says. God "has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor." (Ecclesiastes 5:19) The word that fits is enjoy. You can count crumbs all day, friend, and still not taste the cookie.

explanations.answer: He is kept occupied with joy
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. "For a man seldom considers the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart." (Ecclesiastes 5:20) So God is the One keeping him busy with joy. A man with a glad heart doesn't spend his days counting them.

explanations.answer: He is busy counting his wealth
explanations.explanation: Counting wealth is the money lover's habit, but it's not the reason here. The Teacher says a man seldom considers his days "because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart." (Ecclesiastes 5:20) The thing keeping him busy is joy. No ledger in sight.

explanations.answer: He is too tired from his labor
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say tired. The Teacher says a man seldom considers the days of his life "because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart." (Ecclesiastes 5:20) The reason is joy, not exhaustion. Earlier he did say the worker sleeps sweetly (Ecclesiastes 5:12), but that's another verse.
